Why the unpaginated `GET /v1/tools` returns a `500`, and why not to retry it for other callers'
sake as well as your own.

- **`SKILL.md`, `references/rest-api.md` and `references/troubleshooting.md`: the `500` from the
  tool-collection route is explained rather than called unexplainable, and the route is now
  "don't call this even once".** All three said the `500` "is not explained by anything visible
  to a caller" (`references/rest-api.md` offered no explanation at all). It is deterministic and
  is Danube's own bug: the route is declared
  `-> List[Tool]` while the query behind it selects five columns (`id, name, description, tags,
  service_id`), so every row fails response validation on the four required fields it does not
  carry (`base_url`, `path`, `method`, `version`). Nothing to retry and no parameter changes it.
  The stronger reason to leave the route alone is new: live on 2026-10-23 one such call answered
  `504` after 31.3 s and the whole API was then unreachable for about three minutes — the next
  request came back as the hosting platform's `no_healthy_upstream` page, three `GET /health`
  calls in a row answered `504`, and the `/health` that finally answered reported a seconds-old
  process where a 23-hour-old one had been answering a few minutes before. No deploy explains
  that restart and nothing was filed as an error; whether the call caused it was not
  established, which is also why the files say not to reproduce it to find out. The
  troubleshooting row no longer claims the route cannot be an outage.
- **`references/rest-api.md`: Higgsfield is not one of the catalogue's largest services.** The
  file named its 105 tools beside Vercel's 407 as "the largest in the catalog"; live on
  2026-10-23 ten services carry more — Vercel 407, then Campfire 142, Unusual Whales 132,
  Cal.com 125, Intercom 121, Braze 116, Similarweb 115, Zoom 114, Ramp 112 and Auth0 107 — which
  puts Higgsfield eleventh. The file now carries that list, plus how big "big" actually gets (14
  services at 100 tools or more, Vercel alone past 150) and the note that an `mcp_server`'s count
  moves on its own as the upstream changes (Higgsfield held 101 on 2026-09-20).
- **`SKILL.md`: the `?tools=` group filter is case-insensitive and tolerates spaces.** The file
  warned only that a wrong name is dropped in silence, which left capitalisation looking like one
  of those wrong names. Verified live on 2026-10-23 by counting the `tools/list` reply:
  `?tools=CORE` lists the same 11 as `?tools=core`, `?tools=%20Core%20,%20Workflows%20` the same
  17 as `?tools=core,workflows`, no parameter 33, and `?tools=workfows` on its own 33.
- **`SKILL.md`: the `/v1/stats/public` reading is refreshed** to `{"services": 517, "tools":
  12740, "workflows": 0, "total_executions": 18856}` at 12:16 UTC on 2026-10-23, and the
  four-day deltas from the previous reading replace the five-day ones.

Over REST the `tool_input` wrapper is optional for a tool's parameters and required for
everything that rides beside them, and MCP's `parameters` is not an alias for it.

- **`SKILL.md` and `references/rest-api.md`: `POST /v1/tools/call/{tool_id}` reads a body with
  no `tool_input` key as the tool input itself, so the wrapper is optional for the parameters —
  but `fields`, `confirm_token` and `timeout_seconds` are read only when the body carries that
  key, and without it they are taken for tool parameters and dropped as undeclared with nothing
  saying so.** Both files simply said to wrap the parameters in `tool_input`, leaving an agent
  no way to know which half the wrapper is load-bearing for. Live on 2026-10-22 against
  `Hacker News - Get Top Stories With Content`: `{"limit": 2}` and `{"tool_input": {"limit": 2}}`
  both answered with two stories and `request_params: {"limit": 2}`, while
  `{"limit": 2, "fields": ["[].title"]}` answered `200` with `projection: null` and the whole
  story objects — `fields` echoed back inside `request_params` — against
  `{"tool_input": {"limit": 2}, "fields": ["[].title"]}`, which returned the two titles alone
  with `projection: {"fields": [...], "missing": []}`. The route's own condition is
  `body.get("tool_input", body)` for the input and `"tool_input" in body` for each of those
  three controls (`backend/routers/tools.py`); `max_response_chars` is read in either shape. The
  practical cost is on `confirm_token`, which sent bare never reaches the consent check, so the
  call answers `409` a second time and reads as a token that does not work.
- **Same two files: there is no `parameters` alias on that route, so `{"parameters": {...}}`
  becomes a parameter of that name.** The alias rule the files already carried is MCP's — and
  over REST not even a batch entry takes it — but nothing said the single call does not share it. Live the same day,
  `{"parameters": {"limit": 2}}` on that tool answered `200` with **ten** stories and
  `request_params: {"parameters": {"limit": 2}, "limit": 10}` — the wrapper kept as a parameter
  the row does not declare, so dropped before the upstream request, and the schema's own default
  filling in the `limit` that never arrived. On a tool with a required parameter it fails
  instead, naming what was sent rather than what was meant: `error_type: "missing_parameters"`,
  "Missing required parameters: q. Provided parameters: parameters." (live on
  `HealthData.gov - Autocomplete Dataset Names`).
- **`SKILL.md`: `GET /v1/agents/getting-started`'s byte count is not something to check
  against.** The file cited it as "`200`, 2,727 bytes"; live on 2026-10-22 the same endpoint
  answered `200` with 3,212 bytes, because the three tools under `try_first` are picked from the
  live catalogue and carry their full parameter schemas. The figure and the tools both move
  without the endpoint changing, so the note now says to read what it returns.

The note that is supposed to tell you how to get a file's bytes often has no number in it, and a
per-tool response cap can be larger than the default rather than smaller.

- **`SKILL.md` and `references/troubleshooting.md`: `_meta.file_note` names a
  `max_response_chars` to pass only while that number stays under the MCP layer's 500,000-character
  ceiling.** Both files said it "names the exact number to pass", which holds only for the small
  example they cite. The budget is clamped to 500,000 before it is compared against the file
  (`lift_inline_file`, `mcp/response_shaping.py`: `budget = min(requested_chars or 0,
  absolute_max)` for the inline copy, then `if need <= absolute_max` for the note), so past that
  the note carries no number and says the file "is over the 500,000-character MCP limit", offering the REST
  API, the SDK, the CLI or a smaller `width` instead. Live on 2026-10-21, `Wikimedia Commons - Get
  File Bytes` on `File:Mona Lisa, by Leonardo da Vinci, from C2RMF retouched.jpg` with no `width`
  returned 3,173,276 base64 characters (a 2,379,957-byte 1920x2861 JPEG) and exactly that
  numberless note, while still attaching the image block. Any file much over ~370 KB lands there,
  so the branch without a number is the ordinary case on this tool, not the edge one.
- **`references/rest-api.md`: a tool's own `metadata.max_response_chars` raises the REST ceiling
  for that tool, which is why "call it over REST" actually works.** The file named 2,000,000 as the
  REST clamp with nothing said about the per-tool cap that overrides it. The same call over
  `POST /v1/tools/call/{tool_id}` with no `max_response_chars` sent returned that whole
  3,173,276-character `content_base64` with `truncated: false`, because that tool's row carries
  `metadata.max_response_chars: 12000000` (read live off `GET /v1/tools/wikimedia-commons-get-file-bytes`).
- **`SKILL.md` and `references/troubleshooting.md`: the per-tool default applied on the name path
  is not necessarily a *lower* one.** Both described it as "a publisher's lower per-tool default…
  so trimming below 50000 is normal there" (the trailing clause was SKILL.md's; the
  reference file stopped at "a publisher's lower per-tool default can apply"). The one Danube's
  own registrar writes is higher — the 12,000,000 above, which the MCP layer clamps back to its
  500,000 ceiling — so the figure is read as a different default, never above 500,000 over MCP,
  and it is consulted on the name path only. A publisher may set the key either way on a tool
  they own, so the direction is what you cannot assume.
- **Two smaller corrections the above turned up.** The image block is not unconditional: it is
  attached only while the base64 is at most 5,000,000 characters, and past that the same note
  reads "not shown" instead — which against this tool's 8 MB file ceiling means a file between
  roughly 3.75 MB and 8 MB comes back as metadata alone. And `SKILL.md` and
  `references/rest-api.md` both said a REST batch entry sent without `max_response_chars` gets
  500,000; it gets that tool's own cap when it declares one, because a batch entry runs through
  the same per-tool resolution as a single call.

A Gmail tool this bundle told you to expect does not exist, and the large-service example is
re-measured.

- **`SKILL.md` and `references/troubleshooting.md`: `Gmail - Get Profile` is not a tool you can
  call.** Both files listed it among the Gmail tools a narrowed Google grant refuses. Gmail
  carries six tools and that is not one of them: live on 2026-10-20 `GET
  /v1/services/gmail/tools` returned `Send Email`, `Read Inbox`, `Search Emails`, `Get Email`,
  `Reply to Email` and `Trash Email`, `GET /v1/tools/gmail-get-profile` answered `404`, and an
  exact-name search for it returned those six Gmail rows ahead of two unrelated Klaviyo
  `Get Profile` tools — an existing Gmail row would have been pinned first. Both the definition
  (`backend/utils/composite_tools/gmail.py`) and the executor (`backend/execution/main.py`) for
  it exist, and the `GMAIL_READ_SCOPES` gate in the same file names it, but no catalogue row was
  ever registered, so the gate guards something unreachable. That matters more than a stray
  name, because `execute_tool` resolves an unknown name by searching and runs the nearest
  result: an agent calling `Gmail - Get Profile` off the old list would have resolved to
  `Gmail - Get Email` instead. Both files now name the five refused tools and say the six are
  the whole service; `SKILL.md` also points back to its name-resolution warning.
- **`SKILL.md` and `references/troubleshooting.md`: the 50-tool cut example is re-measured.**
  Higgsfield now carries **105** tool rows, not the 101 recorded for 2026-09-20. Re-verified over
  MCP on 2026-10-20: the default `get_service_tools` call returned 50 and `limit=500` returned
  all 105. The advice is unchanged — pass a big limit rather than reasoning about a service's
  size — and both files now say why, since the count moved by four in a month.

The device flow can mint a key straight into a shared organization, and one credential-returning
tool in the catalogue is named.

- **`SKILL.md` and `references/rest-api.md`: `POST /v1/auth/device/code` takes an `org_id` and
  this bundle never mentioned it.** It accepts an organization **id or slug**, echoes `org_id`
  and `org_name` back (both `null` when none was asked for), and answers an unresolvable one with
  `404 {"error": {"code": "not_found", "message": "Organization not found"}}` before writing
  anything (`backend/routers/device_auth.py`, `_resolve_org_ref` and `create_device_code`, read
  2026-10-19; all three verified live the same day — a shared org's id came back beside
  `"org_name": "Danube"`, an unknown slug `404`, and no `org_id` gave `org_id: null`,
  `org_name: null`). The key the flow then mints is stamped with that organization, so it acts
  for it with no `danube-org-id` header at all — which matters because the rest of this file
  spends a long passage on an agent accidentally ending up outside every shared organization, and
  this is the one point where the workspace can be chosen before the key exists. Both files now
  also say what *no* `org_id` does, since it is easy to assume it is the dangerous choice: the key
  is stamped with the user's personal organization, and that is not the narrowing the
  `danube-org-id` version of it would be — only a shared org switches the request's context
  (`backend/auth.py`, the `is_personal_org(key_org_id) is False` branch), so such a key keeps
  ordinary personal behaviour and still spans every organization the user belongs to.

- **The `200` on `/auth/device/token` was written as `{"api_key": "…"}`.** It carries
  `api_key`, `key_prefix` and `org_id`. Corrected in both files.

- **`references/troubleshooting.md`: a new row for the failure the `org_id` above can produce —
  a poll stuck on `428` while the user insists they entered the code.** Membership is checked at
  the *user's* end, not at code creation: `POST /v1/auth/device/authorize` refuses a non-member
  of the requested organization with a `403` ("This device asked to join an organization you are
  not a member of") and **leaves the code pending**, so the polling side reads `428` with nothing
  naming the cause. The row says to ask what their browser said, that a member can authorize the
  same code so there is nothing to restart, and that an expiry answers `410` rather than `428`.
  It also says to restart with an organization **id** rather than a guessed slug, because a slug
  is whatever was recorded and not the name lowercased: live on 2026-10-19 the org named `Danube`
  answered `404` to the slug `danube`, while the slug `platform` resolved to a *different* org,
  `Danube Catalog`.

- **`SKILL.md`: the unmasked-passthrough paragraph had no named tool, and now has one — plus the
  cause it was missing.** It listed three reasons a secret arrives unmasked (no capture mapping,
  self-hosted custody, a failed store) and not the fourth, a tool declared `passthrough`
  outright. `DigitalOcean Spaces - Spaces Key Create` (`digitalocean-spaces-spaces-key-create`,
  confirmed live in the catalogue 2026-10-19) is one: declared `returns_credential` with a
  `passthrough` capture since 2026-10-17, because DigitalOcean shows a new Spaces key's
  `secret_key` once and masking it left the caller with a key they could not use
  (`backend/mcp_integration/tool_metadata_overrides.py`, commit `20780d09`;
  `execution/credential_capture.py` never captures such a tool by design).

- **`SKILL.md` and `references/rest-api.md`: the `/v1/stats/public` reading was five days old,
  and the sentence beside it quoted a growth rate as if it were steady.** Re-read live at 12:25
  UTC on 2026-10-19: `{"services": 517, "tools": 12737, "workflows": 0, "total_executions":
  18278}`. `services` has not moved since 2026-10-10 and `tools` by three, while the execution
  counter climbed ~2,160 in five days. The "13 in eighteen minutes" sample that stood here is
  now dated to the 2026-10-14 reading it came from and paired with a second one (5 in ~90 s on
  2026-10-19), because the counter moves in bursts and neither sample is the five-day average —
  which is the paragraph's own point, that the number is a sample and not a figure to match.

`retryable` is not "every upstream failure", and a `local_only` tool refuses instantly when the
organization's data-plane agent is not polling.

- **`SKILL.md`: the `retryable` field's set was described as the transient `upstream` types plus
  one caller-side exception. It is neither of those two things.** `retryable` is derived from
  `error_type` by a nine-value table (`backend/execution/fault.py`, `_RETRYABLE` / `is_retryable`,
  read 2026-10-18): seven `upstream` types (`server_error`, `timeout`, `connection_error`,
  `rate_limited`, `upstream_error`, `mcp_transport_error`, `dataplane_timeout`) and **two**
  `caller` types, `plan_rate_limited` and `no_dataplane_agent` — the second of which this file
  did not mention at all. And one `upstream` verdict is deliberately left out:
  `dataplane_execution_failed`, where the customer's data-plane agent ran the call and reported a
  failure without saying which kind, answers `retryable: false` because unclassified is not known
  to be transient. The paragraph now names all nine, names the exception, and says that an error
  site may set the field itself (`attribute_fault` only *defaults* it), so an agent should read
  the field rather than re-derive it from the `fault` verdict.

- **`SKILL.md` and `references/troubleshooting.md`: a new failure an agent calling an
  organization's own tools will actually hit — the data-plane agent being offline.** A
  `local_only` service's calls (and an infrastructure connector stored as `env://` / `vault://`
  references) run on an agent the organization hosts in its own network. If no active agent of
  that organization has polled within **120 seconds**
  (`DATAPLANE_DISPATCH_ONLINE_WINDOW_SECONDS`), `dispatch_and_wait` refuses **before queueing
  anything** rather than waiting out the 60-second dispatch budget: `error_type:
  "no_dataplane_agent"`, `fault: "caller"`, `retryable: true`, message "No data-plane agent is
  online for this organization.", plus a `hint` naming the remedy (`backend/db/dataplane.py`,
  `org_has_online_agent` and the
  fail-fast branch; `backend/tests/unit/test_local_only_execute_branch.py` asserts the dispatch
  row is never created). The skill now tells an agent that nothing ran, that this is the
  organization's agent to restart rather than anything wrong with the call or the tool, and —
  because a *negative* liveness answer is cached for five seconds
  (`OFFLINE_AGENT_CACHE_TTL_SECONDS`) — not to retry in a tight loop, since an immediate second
  attempt is refused from cache without re-checking. The same two places now separate it from the
  two placement refusals that read alike and are **not** retryable: `dataplane_required` (a
  database connector registered on the hosted service without `local_only`; its message ends "No
  query was run") and `driver_missing` (the agent image built without that engine's driver).

A service's slug reads that service's tools but scopes a search to nothing, and the two
catalogue-size numbers on `/health` are equal when nothing is waiting to be embedded.

- **`SKILL.md`, `references/troubleshooting.md` and `references/rest-api.md`: a service slug
  in `search_tools`' `service_id` filter returns an empty page, while the reads beside it accept
  one.** `get_service_tools` and `GET /v1/services/{id}/tools` resolve a service slug as readily
  as its UUID (live 2026-10-17: `gmail` listed that service's tools over MCP and all six over
  REST). The search filter does not: it is matched for exact equality against the `service_id`
  each tool row carries, which is always the UUID, so a slug scopes the search to no service and
  the page comes back empty with nothing naming the filter as the cause. An empty page is also
  what a service with no such tool looks like, which is what makes it read as an answer. Live the
  same minute, `service_id: "gmail"` on the query `send email` answered `[]` over MCP and over
  `GET /v1/tools/search`, while the service's UUID answered with `Gmail - Send Email` first. The
  bundle already pointed at this call twice as the way to ask "can this service do X" without
  `get_service_tools`' 50-tool page, so it was sending agents into it holding the wrong
  identifier. Now stated in the discovery tips, as a troubleshooting row, and beside the curl
  recipe that takes `<SERVICE_ID>`.
- **`SKILL.md`: `/health`'s `index.tools` and `index.lexical_rows` are equal when the index has
  nothing left to embed.** The file called `index.tools` "the narrower count", which reads as
  though a gap is normal and equality is suspect. The lexical index holds every tool row and the
  vector index only the embedded ones, so `index.tools` is never the larger of the two, and live
  on 2026-10-17 both read 12,736 on a process up 23 hours. Reworded, with that reading, so two
  equal numbers are not mistaken for the fields meaning the same thing.

The three tools in the *Wallet & agents* group that don't behave like the rest —
`get_agent_info` refuses an ordinary account outright, `fund_agent_wallet` starts a payment
without checking what kind of account it is, `register_agent` creates a separate one — plus the
plan cap's actual monthly numbers and the pay-as-you-go path past it. The bundle listed all of
this and explained none of it.

- **`SKILL.md` and `references/troubleshooting.md`: `get_agent_info` fails on a human account,
  and the bundle listed it among the read-only calls without ever saying it can refuse.** It
  reads the *agent*
  profile behind the key and refuses anything else with `400` "This endpoint is for agents only.
  Use /v1/users/me for human accounts." — and every account created by signing up in the
  dashboard is a human one, so that is its ordinary answer rather than an edge case. Live over
  this bundle's own connector on 2026-10-16: the call came back as a tool error carrying the REST
  envelope flattened into the message text (`validation_error`), which reads like a platform
  fault and is not one. `get_wallet_balance` is what answers on any account (verified live in the
  same pass: `balance_cents`, `formatted`, `has_wallet`) and `get_spending_limits` gives the caps;
  the `/v1/users/me` the message points at has no MCP tool of its own. A troubleshooting row now
  carries the symptom, and the capability bullet says which call to reach for instead.
- **`SKILL.md`: `fund_agent_wallet` has no such check, and its two methods top up two different
  wallets.** On the MCP surface the "agents only" refusal exists on the agent-info route alone,
  so the one tool here that starts a payment is the one that never asks what kind of account it
  is — it works on a human account, and both methods act on the caller's own wallets. (Neither
  moves money by itself: the card path returns a Stripe URL someone must complete, the crypto
  path an address.) `method: "card_checkout"` opens a Stripe checkout that lands in the **credits**
  wallet (the cents balance `get_wallet_balance` reads and a priced tool charges), while
  `method: "crypto"` returns the USDC deposit address; the `balance_usdc` in the response is the
  USDC figure either way, so after a card checkout the number handed back is not the balance that
  moves. Now stated, with the reminder to confirm before either call.
- **`SKILL.md`: `register_agent` creates a separate, unconnected account, and its
  `getting_started` block never arrives over MCP.** It is the only tool here that sends no
  credential at all, so nothing links what it creates to the caller: a new profile under a
  generated `agent-…@agents.danubeai.com` address (the `operator_email` is contact detail, not a
  login), normally its own personal organization (that step is best-effort), the free tier, and
  an **unrestricted** API key returned once in the tool result — a key created this way carries no
  per-key scoping, so what bounds it is the new account's own organization membership at the
  tool-call boundary rather than a permission list — with no dashboard sign-in and no second
  copy. It is therefore not a
  way to give an agent its own access to the user's services — it reaches none of them. The
  backend's response also carries a `getting_started` block (free tier, endpoints, three
  credential-free tools, what to read next) that the MCP result has no field for, so over MCP it
  is dropped with nothing said; `GET /v1/agents/getting-started` serves the same block and needs
  no key (live 2026-10-16: `200`, 2,727 bytes, keys `free_tier`, `endpoints`, `try_first`,
  `read_next`, `steps`). Both facts are new to the bundle.
- **All three files: the plan cap had no numbers, and reaching it does not always refuse.** The
  monthly quota is 5,000 successful calls per UTC calendar month on free, 50,000 on pro, 250,000
  on team and uncapped on enterprise (legacy `starter` 10,000), and `error.details.usage` names
  the one that was hit (`tier`, `limit`, `current_usage`, `remaining`) — the bundle described the
  `429`'s shape and the per-minute limiter next to it without ever giving these. Past the cap an
  account that has opted into pay-as-you-go and holds the cent is let *through* on a direct tool
  call instead, charged from the credits wallet in blocks of ten calls per cent, with REST
  stamping `billing: {"mode": "overage", "charged_cents": N}` beside `cost_cents` and `N` at 0 on
  the nine calls an earlier cent already covered. Over MCP that `billing` block is dropped and
  `_meta.cost_cents` is the only trace. Workflows and chat keep the strict cap, so the same call
  can run through `execute_tool` and be refused as a workflow step — which is also what a `429`
  on a pay-as-you-go account tells you about the opt-in or the wallet.

`list_services` grew a detail level that empties the rows above a limit of 25, it drops every
service the catalogue reports with no tools, and the `-32602` failure the bundle warned about is
fixed. All three came from the same commit (2026-09-28) and none had reached the skill.

- **`SKILL.md` and `references/troubleshooting.md`: a `limit` over 25 silently empties
  `description` and `url`.** `list_services` takes a third parameter, `detail` — `"auto"`
  (default), `"full"` or `"compact"` — and `auto` returns the full form up to a `limit` of 25 and
  the compact form above it. The switch is on the limit asked for, not on the number of rows
  returned, and compact empties the two fields rather than dropping the keys, so nothing in the
  answer says the level changed. Live on 2026-10-15 one query answered with full descriptions at
  `limit: 25` and with `description: ""` and `url: null` on every row at `limit: 26`. The
  capability table now shows the parameter, and both files say a page of blank descriptions is
  the detail level rather than a catalogue without any. Also noted: an unrecognised `detail` is a
  loud error ("detail must be one of auto, full, compact", live), which is the opposite of the
  `?tools=` group filter's silent drop the bundle already documents.
- **A service the listing finds no tools for is left out entirely.**
  So the page can be shorter than the limit while more results exist, and the service searched
  for by name can be the missing one. The condition is narrower than "the catalogue says 0": the
  catalogue count must be exactly `0` *and*, below the compact threshold, a live check of the
  service's tool list must come back empty too — above it that check is skipped, so the same
  query can return a different *set* of services at `limit: 25` and `limit: 26`. A count that
  arrived `null` is not dropped at all (`None == 0` is False); it survives reading
  `tool_count: 0`, un-recounted in a compact listing. Live on 2026-10-15, `GET /v1/services?query=Day AI` over
  REST returned ten rows of which `Day AI`, `Read AI` and `Peec AI` carried `tool_count: 0`, and
  `list_services(query: "Day AI")` over MCP returned exactly the other seven — `Day AI` itself
  absent from a search for it. `Day AI` is an `mcp_server` row with no tools registered, i.e. the
  `needs_mcp_oauth` case the bundle already covers, so the two are now cross-referenced.
- **The `-32602` "Invalid request parameters" failure is fixed, and the bundle was still telling
  agents to work around it.** A page holding a service whose `tool_count` arrived `null` used to
  fail the MCP layer's own `Service` model, which declares that field an `int`; the count is now
  coerced to `0` before the model sees it (`mcp/mcp_server.py`, 2026-09-28). `query: "Day AI"` —
  the query both files named as having failed five times running on 2026-09-15 and "still failing
  on 2026-09-23" — returns normally (live 2026-10-15). The old reading is kept in one sentence,
  because the MCP server publishes no build or boot time and a caller cannot tell from outside

  timezone (default `UTC`), nothing firing until `schedule_enabled` is `true`, a `400` for

Three things an agent runs into while wiring the connection up by hand, none of them written down
before: which verb the MCP endpoint answers, how to read its `401`s, and the key header that works
against the MCP server but not against the REST API.

- **Probing `https://mcp.danubeai.com/mcp` with `curl` has traps that read like a bad key.**
  `references/troubleshooting.md` gains a working probe and how to read what comes back, all
  verified live on 2026-10-03. POST is the only verb that does anything — a `GET` with a valid key
  answers `405 Method Not Allowed`, and the `Allow: DELETE, POST` beside it is not a second route
  (`DELETE` answers `405 Method Not Allowed: Session termination not supported`). A JSON-RPC
  `initialize` POST replies as `text/event-stream` (`event: message` then a `data:` line,
  `serverInfo` `Danube MCP Server` 4.0.5), so piping it to `jq` fails on a perfectly healthy
  server; send `Accept: application/json, text/event-stream` or no `Accept` at all, since
  `Accept: application/json` alone is a `406`. The two `401`s differ by message — `API key
  required. Provide 'danube-api-key' header or 'Authorization: Bearer <api_key>'.` for no key,
  `Invalid API key` for a rejected one — and only the unauthenticated case hides a wrong URL:
  authentication short-circuits ahead of routing, so with no key a mistyped path answers `401`
  (`GET /sse` does, and no SSE transport is served), while the same path **with** a working key
  reaches routing and answers `404 Not Found`. A REST path on that host is the one informative
  `404`: `This endpoint is not available on the MCP server.`
- **`Authorization: Bearer <key>` is accepted by the MCP server and unreliable on the REST API.**
  Both files now say so, and say what the two failures look like. The MCP server reads the key
  from either header; `/v1/*` reads only `danube-api-key`, and a key sent as a Bearer token is
  either refused or ignored depending on the route's auth. `/v1/tools/search`, which requires a
  key, answered `401 {"error":{"code":"unauthorized","message":"API key required"}}` — a message
  that reads as "you sent no key" when the key was simply in the header REST reserves for a
  dashboard JWT. `/v1/services?limit=3`, whose auth is optional, answered `200` with byte-for-byte
  the same 1,616,675 bytes as the call made with no credentials at all, so the key is dropped in
  silence and anything it would have unlocked is quietly absent. That second case is the one worth
  knowing: it has no error to notice.
- **The service-listing context bill, re-measured.** `references/rest-api.md` warns that
  `GET /services?limit=3` returns the whole catalogue; its figure was 496 services and ~1.5 MB
  from 2026-09-16. On 2026-10-03 the same call returned 516 services and 1.6 MB, 55 fields a row,
  so the number is current again and labelled as a floor that grows with the catalogue.

The consent handshake has a second trigger, and the bundle named only the first. Everywhere it
appeared — the guardrail, both reference files and the skill card — a `confirmation_required`
meant one thing: "the API key has `require_confirmation` set". Since the infrastructure
connectors shipped (Danube #934, 2026-09-26) that is no longer the whole rule, and an agent
holding the old one draws the wrong conclusion in both directions.

- **A tool can demand the handshake from every caller, whatever the key says.**
  `enforce_consent` (`backend/services/consent.py:211-287`) fires when *either* the key carries
  `require_confirmation` *or* `policy_requires_consent` does, and the second needs nothing from
  the account. Two cases reach it, a tool row marked `metadata.require_confirmation` and a write
  on a connected system's generic request tool; both are bounded below. The first is
  every **write** tool of the catalog's infrastructure connectors — thirteen across eight of the
  seventeen services, stamped by `backend/scripts/register_infra_connectors.py:73-78` whose own
  comment reads "writes also always need a confirm_token, whatever the caller's API key says":
  `PostgreSQL - Execute Statement`, `MySQL - Execute Statement`,
  `ClickHouse - Execute Statement`, `Redis - Set`, `Redis - Delete`, `Redis - Expire`,
  `Apache Kafka - Produce Message`, `Kubernetes - Restart Rollout`,
  `Kubernetes - Scale Deployment`, `AWS DynamoDB - Put Item`, `AWS DynamoDB - Update Item`,
  `AWS DynamoDB - Delete Item` and `AWS Lambda - Invoke`. All thirteen announce the requirement in their own published
  description, which is what lets an agent see it before it calls: seven word it "every call
  needs an explicit confirmation" (verified live in the catalog on
  `PostgreSQL - Execute Statement`, `Redis - Set`, `Redis - Delete` and `Redis - Expire`), the
  Kubernetes and AWS six say "with a confirmation on every call" or just "with a confirmation".
  An organization's own connected-system copy of the same ops carries the flag as well
  (`services/connect_flow.py:867`); the one documented way out is an admin setting that system's
  policy to `writes: "allowed"` (`consent.py:118-123`), and a key carrying `require_confirmation`
  would still ask. The second case is narrower than "a connected system whose policy asks for
  consent": `policy_requires_consent` reaches it only for the generic `<Service> - Request` tool
  (or a promoted request row) and reads `http.writes` (`access_policy.py:475-477`), so a write
  through a connected database's `Query` tool does not trigger it.
- **So a handshake on a key with the setting off is not a contradiction.** The bundle's line
  "The API key has `require_confirmation` set" invited exactly that reading, and the
  no-prompt row's "the gate is ... off unless someone turned it on" is now scoped to the
  key-side trigger, which is the only one that clause was ever true of.
- **The 409 carries a `reason`, and the bundle had never listed the field.**
  `error.details.reason` is `"api_key"` or `"service_policy"` (`consent.py:226`, `:285`), and on
  the second the message gains "This service's access policy requires a confirmation for every
  write." `references/rest-api.md`'s field list — token, `expires_in`, `tool_id`, `tool_name`,
  `method`, parameters — now carries `reason` too, and both files say to read it by precedence:
  `consent.py:226` gives the key-side trigger the label whenever it applies, so `"service_policy"`
  is the value that tells you something (the key does *not* have the setting on) while
  `"api_key"` leaves open whether the tool would have asked anyway. The same details dict reaches
  a batch entry verbatim (`routers/tools.py:1078-1085`), so the batch passages in
  `rest-api.md` and `troubleshooting.md` gained `reason` and lost their key-only framing too.
- **Over MCP you cannot tell which fired.** `mcp/mcp_server.py:1982-1994` rebuilds `_meta` from
  the backend's `details` with `confirm_token`, `expires_in` and `parameters` only, dropping
  `reason`, and the text it composes is its own rather than the backend's message. Stated so an
  agent on MCP treats the handshake as the tool's requirement instead of inferring an account
  setting it cannot see.

  write prose and hand it `allowed_tool_ids` and a Danube-hosted model decides which of those

  "instructions-mode workflow" and `allowed_tool_ids` appeared in exactly one troubleshooting row

  required") and an unreadable id ("Tool not found: …"), read from

  (`WorkflowExecutionResponse`, `backend/models/workflows.py`; `None` in template mode), while
  `step_results` holds only the tool calls it made along the way — and *A failed run is not an

Workspaces and sharing with an organization, plus three side routes that now treat a tool you
cannot see the way they treat one that isn't there, and a JSON body Danube used to mistake
for an MCP envelope.

- **A tool you are not allowed to see reads as unrated, not as forbidden.** Danube #936
  (merged 2026-09-27) put the visibility check on the routes beside execution.
  `get_tool_ratings` / `GET /v1/ratings/tool/{id}` answers such a tool with
  `{"avg_rating": null, "rating_count": 0}` — byte for byte what a genuinely unrated tool
  returns, so the zero has a fourth cause now. The check is against the *caller*, which makes
  the key matter on a route the reference called "no key needed": read it anonymously and your
  own organization's internal tools come back unrated. Both reference files and the SKILL's
  quality-signal section said this endpoint "validates nothing"; it validates the id's shape
  first now, so that wording is corrected too.
- **`submit_rating`'s `404` gained a second meaning.** The same status and the same
  "No tool with id …" message now also answer a tool on a service hidden from you, and
  `report_tool` refuses one the same way. The old advice — re-resolve with `search_tools` and
  submit against the id you get back — loops forever on that case, because search hides the
  same tool, so the skill now says to stop when the re-resolve comes up empty.
- **A tool whose own JSON has a `content` key is ordinary JSON.** `Google Drive - Download File
  Content` answers `{"content": "<file text>", "mimeType": …}`. Danube #927 recognises the MCP
  `{content: [...], isError}` envelope only when `content` is a list, so that body now lands
  whole in `result.data`. Before it, the string was walked one character at a time and the call
  failed with `'str' object has no attribute 'get'` **after the backend had already run it and
  logged it as a success** — which is why the note tells you to treat such a call as done rather
  than retry it against an older deployment.
- **`list_workflows` has a fourth `scope`: `"org"`.** Danube #954 (merged 2026-09-27) added the
  workflows a colleague shared with the user's organization, so the scopes are `"mine"`, `"org"`,
  `"public"` and `"all"`, and `"all"` now orders them yours, then the organization's, then
  public. Rows carry `owned_by_you: true` or `shared_with_org: true` with `org_name`. The bundle
  had never documented `scope` at all; it does now, with `GET /workflows/my?include_org=true` as
  the `curl` equivalent. Verified live on 2026-09-28: `scope: "org"` is accepted and answers
  normally, where it used to come back `scope must be "mine", "public", or "all"`.
- **Sharing a workflow or a skill with an organization is a move through its own route.**
  `POST /v1/workflows/{id}/share` and `/unshare` (and the same pair on `/v1/skills/{id}`) change
  visibility between `private` and `internal` keeping the id and the link; only the **author** may
  do either, an organization's own admin gets a `403`, and a `PATCH` that moves `visibility` into
  or out of `internal` is refused with a `400` naming those routes. `GET
  /v1/workflows/{id}/share-check` reports per step whether members can see that tool and whose credential the step
  would run with, and `/share` refuses with a `400` naming tools members can't use. None of this
  was in the bundle.
- **The `danube-org-id` header can narrow a request to no organization at all.** Danube #953
  brought workspaces: naming the account's own *personal* organization in that header puts the
  request outside every shared one, and its internal tools, shared credentials, credential rules,
  parameter defaults, skills and context layer all drop out with nothing in the response to say
  why. Read live on 2026-09-28: one key's `GET /v1/context` returned the organization's layer and
  six skills with no header, and no organization layer and zero skills with that account's own
  personal org id in the header. The bundle said only that the header "chooses one explicitly and
  wins over the key", which invites exactly that mistake; it now says to send no header unless the
  user named a shared organization, and the context section no longer reads a missing
  organization layer with no `note` as "the organization has written none". Over MCP the trap is
  closed at the server: since 2026-09-27 it forwards an organization the client asked for, or a
  shared one the key is bound to, but never the key's personal-org fallback.

An MCP tool listing is a summary now, and three refusals an agent would otherwise misread.

- **`search_tools` and `get_service_tools` over MCP no longer carry the full schema.** From
  Danube #885 and #887 they default to `detail="summary"`: identity, a description truncated at
  300 characters, `parameters` reduced to `name -> {type, required}` (plus a short `enum`),
  `readiness`, and `has_tips` in place of the tips text. Gone from a listing entry are parameter
  descriptions, `json_schema`, `default` and bounds; `reliability` keeps five keys;
  `configuration_url` appears only when the tool is not ready; and the pricing and deprecation
  keys appear only when they are set, so their absence now means "free" and "not deprecated"
  rather than missing data. `describe_tool(tool_id)` is where the schema lives, and
  `detail="full"` restores the old shape at about four and a half times the size (19,422
  characters against 89,696 for the same 20 Apollo results). The file also now says that the
  declared `output` and the plumbing fields were never on an MCP listing at any detail level —
  the MCP layer's tool model does not declare them — so `detail="full"` is not the way to get
  them. The
  skill had been telling agents the opposite — that all three MCP listings carry the schema, that
  `json_schema` rides on every search result with an explicit `null` when absent, and that every
  result carries four pricing fields — which on the default path is now wrong three times over.
  REST is unchanged, and the file says so.
- **`auth_required` has three reasons, and one of them makes storing a key pointless.** Beside
  `missing` there is `rejected` (Danube holds a credential and the service refused it — reconnect,
  don't re-store) and, from Danube #888, `org_policy`: the user's organization has a credential
  rule for that service. Under `mode: "shared"` the org requires its own shared credential and
  has none, so a key stored for this user is ignored and an owner or admin has to add it; under
  `mode: "personal"` asking this user for their own key is right after all.
- **A Google connection can be connected and still refuse.** Danube's own Google client asks only
  for scopes Google approves without a paid security review, so on a connection whose grant was
  recorded under that narrowed client (from 2026-09-26) Gmail's `Send Email` works while
  `Read Inbox`, `Search Emails`, `Get Email`, `Reply to Email`, `Get Profile` and `Trash Email`
  are refused up front, and Drive sees only files Danube created or opened. An older grant is
  treated as holding the full scope list and is unaffected. It arrives as `permission_denied` /
  `fault: caller` — the same code as the enterprise access policy, with a different fix:
  reconnect with the user's own Google Cloud project. The skill previously explained that code
  only as the access policy, and called Google the only place a ready tool refuses; Slack's
  `missing_scope` and `not_in_channel` do the same, and the file now says so.

- **Save a parameter default without asking first.** When a service needs an identifier the
  account always uses (Vercel `teamId`, a Sentry org slug) and a call with it has succeeded,
  call `set_parameter_defaults` right away and tell the user in one line what you saved. The
  skill used to say to wait for the user to confirm, and in practice no default was ever saved.
  Saved defaults now appear on the service's page in the Danube dashboard, where the user can
  remove them; the dashboard no longer lets a person type them in.

Two corrections an agent can hit head-on, plus the enterprise edits that were sitting in the
bundle unpublished.

The one that changes what an agent should *do*: on the in-VPC data-plane path, a credential
reference is not merely supported, it is the only form that works. The control plane strips every
plaintext value out of the dispatch it sends the agent — the secret never leaves Danube, only the
fact that it exists — and the agent then refuses the call with
`credential_reference_unresolved` (`fault: caller`) rather than calling with no auth. The skill
had been saying the opposite, telling an agent to store the value when in doubt, which on one of
those services is guaranteed to fail. It also now says where that applies: since 2026-09-24 a
`local_only` MCP server runs its calls *and* its tool discovery through the agent, so the
long-standing "`mcp_server` services read the stored string as the secret" rule holds for a
hosted MCP service and is reversed for a `local_only` one. `references/troubleshooting.md` gains
the refusal as its own row, next to — and explicitly distinguished from — the opposite mistake
already documented there (a reference stored on a service that doesn't resolve one, which the
provider answers with a `401`).

The second is stale detail in the curl reference: registering a service for an organization takes
a fifth `source`, `database`, and `local_only` is no longer HTTP-only. The `400` that reference
attributed to "an MCP server asked to be `local_only`" is actually raised for a *local (stdio)*
server whatever visibility was asked for, and the one reason it was missing is the database rule —
on the hosted service a database connector must be `local_only`, because the query runs where the
DSN lives, and any other visibility is refused at registration rather than at call time. The
route's `400` list now names both, with the messages each one carries.

Every failed tool call now tells an agent whose failure it was, and the skill had no idea: this release documents the `fault` / `error_type` / `retryable` fields, the five reliability fields that came with them, the ceiling on a stored result handle, and the per-call timeout knob. It also catches `batch_execute_tools` up with the three fixes it got on 2026-09-10 — `fields` per entry, an execution handle per element, and a projection path that survives being copied out of the redaction report — and, from a later pass, routed curl users off a per-tool endpoint that was unusable at the time (since fixed — see the fourteenth pass below), writes down how the consent handshake behaves inside a batch (and where it can't be completed at all), and says plainly what that handshake does *not* classify as destructive. It further covers what an agent sees in the seconds after a service is connected — an empty tool list that means "not yet", not "none" — the response shapes the curl reference had left to guesswork, and how to read the `upgrade_url` a plan cap hands back. A last pass writes down what a publisher-priced tool's refusal actually looks like — the message, the two figures beside it and the one page both top-up links reach — corrects the consent gate's publisher flag from something that adds to the method test to something that overrides it in both directions, and re-probes the two standing Danube-side defects, naming the cause of one and sharpening the diagnosis of the other. A tenth pass writes down the two silent size caps an agent runs into while reading rather than executing: `get_service_tools` returns at most 50 tools over MCP with nothing in the answer to say a larger service was cut, and `fetch_result` hands back at most 50000 characters of a stored result unless asked for more — both of them defaults an agent can raise once it knows they are there. An eleventh pass documents the one budget every agent spends and none of them could see: Danube's own rate limits — what they are per plan, that they are counted per API key *and per URL path*, so the free plan's sixty a minute is sixty per tool rather than sixty in all, and that a batch is a single request against them while still spending the plan quota entry by entry. Documents two platform behaviours that shipped after 8.1.5 was written, both of which change what an agent sees coming back from `execute_tool` — and one of which an agent following 8.1.5 would most likely have misread as a broken tool.

- **Credential values are masked out of tool responses.** Danube now runs each tool response through a redactor before it reaches the caller, the logs, or the execution record: anything that reads as a secret (API keys, tokens, passwords, connection strings) comes back as `[REDACTED:<FIELD>]`. 8.1.5 said nothing about this, so an agent that asked a tool for something credential-shaped and got a placeholder had every reason to call the tool broken and `report_tool` it — the same false-failure shape the truncation guidance already exists to prevent. SKILL.md now states that masking is policy and describes the report precisely: an exact `count`, a `fields` list capped at the first 50 (`path` / `key` / `rule`), and a `mode`. The presence rule differs by transport and is now stated as such — over MCP `_meta.redaction` is absent when nothing was masked, while over REST the key is always present and `null` (`ToolExecutionResponse.redaction` is `Optional[...] = None` and the endpoint doesn't exclude nulls), so the guidance is to test the value, not the key. Cursors and identifiers are exempt by key name, so paging keeps working.
- **Tools that mint a credential mostly no longer hand it to the agent — but not always, and the exceptions matter more than the rule.** Where Danube can capture it, the new value is stored as the user's credential for the target service and then masked, with `_meta.redaction.stored_credentials` naming the `service_id`, `field` and `credential_type` it landed under. Where it can't — a `returns_credential` tool with no capture mapping, a self-hosted deployment where custody stays in the customer's environment, or a store that failed — the secret comes back **completely unmasked**, with `_meta.redaction.passthrough_reason` (top-level `redaction.passthrough_reason` over REST) saying why and `count: 0` beside it. An early draft of this release described that class as short-lived handoff tokens (a Plaid link token, a Clerk sign-in token); review against the live specs showed it also carries durable secrets — `plaid.yaml`'s `exchange_public_token` returns the durable access token this way, and `sent.yaml`'s webhook-signing-secret rotation likewise. The skill now says to treat anything arriving unmasked as a live secret rather than context to echo or reuse.
- **A parameter the tool's schema doesn't declare is dropped before the request is made.** It never reaches the provider, and on a failed call the error message now ends with a note naming it. Without that, "the upstream ignored my value" and "the value never left Danube" produce identical output and the natural reading sends the investigation upstream, where there is nothing to find. Two limits found in review and reflected in the text: the note in the error message is the **only** caller-visible report — the internal envelope's `dropped_unknown_params` list is stripped by `ToolExecutionResponse`, so no REST or MCP response carries it and an earlier draft telling agents to read that field would have sent them looking for something that isn't there — and the dropping happens on the HTTP execution path only, so an MCP-backed tool forwards undeclared parameters to its provider unfiltered. Both reference files and SKILL.md's discovery tips now scope the claim and point at the message, quoting the note in full (including its plural wording, which changes when more than one name is dropped) so an agent matching on the text actually finds it, and treat a dropped name as a sign the tool's schema may be missing a parameter the provider supports — worth a `[suggestion]` report rather than a workaround.

Documents four live behaviours the skill had never mentioned, each of which an agent following 8.1.4 would have misread — three of them as a failure that wasn't one.

- **The free-tier cap on AI-powered workflows.** A free-tier account gets 5 lifetime *successful* workflow runs that use a Danube-hosted AI step; past that, `execute_workflow` refuses the run with HTTP `402` before any step executes, so nothing partially ran and no execution row exists. The skill said nothing about `402`. Worse, `402` isn't in the backend's status→code map, so the error envelope's `code` reads `internal_error` — the exact shape that makes an agent conclude Danube broke and `report_tool` it. The skill now keys on the status and the message text and warns about that `code`. `references/troubleshooting.md` also names the nine hosted tools that count (Screenshot doesn't), notes that calling them directly with `execute_tool` is never gated, and flags that an **instructions-mode** workflow trips the cap by merely listing a hosted-AI tool in `allowed_tool_ids`, whether or not a step calls it. (Shipped 2026-08-31 in the backend; both columns migration 104 adds were confirmed present in production this cycle.)
- **A failed run is not an error status.** A workflow whose steps fail comes back `200` with `status: "failed"` in the body; only a run that never started is an HTTP error. An agent treating 2xx as success silently books failed runs as successful ones. Now stated in SKILL.md and in `references/rest-api.md`'s status table.
- **A long run is not a failed one either.** `execute_workflow` answers `status: "running"` with an `execution_id` when the run outlives the request that started it — not cancelled, not failed. Re-running it duplicates every write the first run makes. Now documented as poll-`get_workflow_execution`, never re-run. Note this response is generated by the MCP server's own client timeout: over `curl` there is no Danube `504`, just a timeout, so the REST guidance says to treat any timeout the same way. `references/rest-api.md` also shows supplying your own fresh `execution_id` UUID over REST — the MCP tool mints one for you, but over `curl` a timeout with no id up front leaves the in-flight run unaddressable.
- **How to read an `execute_tool` result.** `{result, _meta}` once a call reaches a tool, with the parsed JSON at `result.data` rather than `result.content[0].text`; `_meta` is absent when the lookup itself failed, so don't index it blindly. Oversized payloads are trimmed — a JSON array at element boundaries (still parseable), plain text mid-string with an inline note — and flagged via `_meta.truncated` / `_meta.truncation_note`, raisable with `max_response_chars` (default 50000, hard max 500000, though a publisher may set a lower per-tool default) or paged with `_meta.cursor`. Documented so a trimmed-but-valid result isn't mistaken for a malformed one and reported as broken, including that `batch_execute_tools` puts `truncated`/`cursor` at each element's top level rather than under `_meta`.

`references/rest-api.md`'s new workflow status table also documents `404` (unknown workflow, private-and-not-yours, or a malformed id) rather than folding those into `400`, which is now scoped to what actually lands there: an execution record that couldn't be created, in practice a reused or unparseable `execution_id`.

Also corrected: that same section no longer says to read a top-level `detail` key — every API error uses the `error.code` / `error.message` / `error.details` envelope the same file already documents — and notes that a few backend handlers (Firecrawl scrape/crawl, Drive download) cap content server-side, so truncation is not purely an MCP-layer concern.
